content_html:
Entropy

Entropy is a universal tendency In a closed system, entropy (disorder) tends to increase. Energy spontaneously spreads out; structures decay unless energy is supplied to maintain them. The implication is that the “default” direction of the universe is toward heat death and disorder.

But life is not a closed system. Organisms and cultures draw energy from the sun, food, or other sources. Life maintains order by exporting disorder - it locally builds complexity while increasing entropy globally. Beavers’ dams, human agriculture, digital technologies - all create local order (structured niches) by consuming energy and producing waste heat. Earthworms leave enriched soil, beavers leave wetlands - these modifications persist, scaffolding faster adaptations for descendants. Each generation inherits not just genes, but also altered niches (ecological) and symbol systems (cultural), which speed up further innovation.

However, acceleration is energy-intensive. Cultural complexity (e.g., cities, the internet) requires massive energy throughput. More complexity = faster entropy export. Civilisation is effectively an entropy accelerator - burning through energy gradients to maintain local order. The paradox here is that evolution appears to speed up (cultural acceleration), but it does so by aligning with entropy: using available energy faster to build fragile order that will eventually decay.

At the local scale, ecological & cultural inheritance allow rapid, layered accumulation of complexity (accelerating change). But at a universal scale all such complexity increases entropy production overall. Evolutionary acceleration is like a flame: a highly ordered, self-organising process that exists only because it consumes fuel and spreads heat (entropy). Entropy sets the background rule: decay is inevitable in closed systems. Ecological and cultural inheritance let organisms temporarily outrun decay by scaffolding faster innovation, but this “acceleration” is achieved only by burning energy gradients - ultimately reinforcing entropy. Evolution and entropy are not opposed: life and culture are entropy engines that create local order while driving global disorder.

Closed system

The Second Law of Thermodynamics is formulated for closed systems (no energy/matter exchange). But in practice local systems (organisms, planets) are open: they take in energy, export waste. The universe as a whole is often treated as “closed,” since by definition it has no “outside.”

Over cosmic timescales, energy gradients smooth out, entropy maximises, and no work can be done. Expansion accelerates this, leading to “thermal equilibrium.” So complexity (life, culture, stars, galaxies) is a temporary pocket - like a flame in a darkening room.

If universes can bud off, recycle, or interact, then “closure” breaks. Entropy might also reset in “big bounce” cosmologies. Information conservation in black holes, or vacuum fluctuations, might suggest that deeper structures may permit renewal. Even if the universe is closed overall, organisms and cultures exploit local openness (sunlight, chemical gradients). Cultural inheritance accelerates change precisely because we extract and burn through these gradients faster. If the universe is closed, acceleration just hastens entropy’s levelling. If not, we may be part of a larger cycle, entropy may be just one phase where order and disorder co-create across levels we can’t yet perceive.

The assumption of closure makes entropy look like the final horizon of meaning, but if the universe is not closed, entropy becomes a local rule within a broader dynamic - possibly one that includes renewal, cycles, or unknown forms of “reconstruction.”

Select: we assume closure.
Change: physics may revise that assumption (e.g., multiverse, bounce models).
Reconstruct: meaning shifts if entropy is not the final word.

Dimensions

When we talk about ‘order and disorder co-create across levels we can’t yet perceive,’ physics and mathematics often describe this in multiple dimensions, some perceptible, some hidden. Our everyday exists in 3 spatial dimensions (length, width, height) plus a time dimension (treated differently, but together with space in relativity). So we live in a 4-dimensional spacetime.

General relativity works in 4D, but mathematically it can be written in any number of dimensions. In string theory / M-theory, consistency requires 10 dimensions (superstring) or 11 dimensions (M-theory) and 6–7 of these are “compactified” (rolled up at the Planck scale, invisible at human scales). Some theories propose spacetime itself is emergent from lower-dimensional information. In mathematics, dimensions are simply independent variables, it can model spaces of 2D, 4D, 100D, or infinite-dimensional spaces. Physics uses them pragmatically, extra dimensions often emerge naturally in equations seeking unification or symmetry, because higher dimensions simplify the maths by making forces or particles manifestations of geometry. What looks like separate forces in 4D may be geometry in 10D. Entropy, quantum entanglement, and even black-hole physics are sometimes best described using higher-dimensional frameworks.

In our familiar 3+1 spacetime, we see multiple forces: gravity, electromagnetism, strong & weak nuclear forces. These look very different: gravity curves spacetime, electromagnetism uses fields, the nuclear forces involve exchanges of gluons and W/Z bosons… the mathematics looks fragmented - many different “rules.” But in higher dimensions, forces can emerge as geometry - what looked like two forces is just different aspects of one higher-dimensional geometry. This principle inspires modern work: perhaps all forces are just shadows of geometry in a higher-dimensional space.

In string theory: particles aren’t points but vibrating strings, and their different vibration modes = different particles (electron, photon, gluon). But the math only works consistently in 10 dimensions (9 space + 1 time) - the “extra” 6 spatial dimensions are compactified (rolled up very small). The shape of those compactified dimensions determines the particle spectrum: masses, charges, interactions. So what seems like dozens of particle types may just be different resonances of strings in higher-dimensional geometry.

Symmetry and geometry

Symmetry and geometry are the deepest threads that tie mathematics, physics, and life together. Since Euclid, geometry describes space: shapes, lengths, angles. With Riemann and Einstein, geometry became dynamic: curved spacetime explains gravity. Geometry isn’t just abstract: it literally is the fabric in which matter and energy move.

A symmetry = transformation that leaves something unchanged (e.g., rotate a circle, it looks the same). Every continuous symmetry has a conserved quantity.conservation of momentum, whether it is time translation symmetry → conservation of energy, or rotation symmetry → conservation of angular momentum.

Organisms exploit geometry: body plans, sensory systems, and even DNA structures are shaped by geometric constraints. Brains build models of the world using symmetry; neurons generalise across rotated/shifted inputs (visual invariances), memory and prediction rely on detecting conserved patterns.

We often seek beauty through symmetry (architecture, music, design) but also growth through symmetry-breaking (novelty, asymmetry). Perfect symmetry = total sameness, but that’s sterile. Broken symmetry = creates structure. In the early universe, a more symmetric force “broke” into the four distinct forces we see today. Order emerges from symmetry-breaking. Life and mind thrive by detecting, exploiting, and breaking symmetries inside the universe’s geometric framework.

Stable emergent regularities

If symmetry and geometry organise physics, are they fundamental, or do they themselves emerge from something more basic? In General Relativity, spacetime geometry is dynamic: matter/energy tell spacetime how to curve, but in quantum gravity approaches, geometry may not be fundamental at all, geometry emerges from networks of quantised relations, and smooth spacetime emerges from patterns of quantum entanglement on a lower-dimensional boundary. Tensor networks also show explicitly how entanglement structure can generate emergent space with geometric properties.

What looks like a fundamental symmetry can be broken by conditions of the system. Symmetries often appear at large scales even if they’re absent at the smallest, for example, rotational symmetry of fluid equations arises even though molecules interact asymmetrically. Some physicists propose that information - yes/no distinctions, entanglement patterns - is more basic than geometry - geometry is an emergent approximation of deeper discrete relations. Just as temperature is not fundamental but emerges from particle motion, spacetime geometry may be a macroscopic variable arising from microstructure.

The fact that brains exploit geometry and symmetry may itself hint that these are stable emergent regularities: brains latch onto invariants that persist across scales. If geometry and symmetry are emergent, they are still reliable enough to be the scaffolding for life and thought. Geometry emerges from networks of relations (entanglement, spin networks, causal sets), symmetry emerges from dynamics, averaging, and phase transitions; both are likely macroscopic regularities that make our universe intelligible - but they do not represent the ultimate substrate.
